newsitem.title: Egypt: Egypt names suspects in church attack.
newsitem.headline: Egypt names suspects in church attack.

text.p: Egyptian police named on Saturday five men suspected of massacring 10 Coptic Christians in an attack on a church in southern Egypt on Wednesday and appealed to the public for information on their whereabouts.

State television showed photographs of the men, four of them local men in their late 20s, and described them as terrorists -- the usual term for the Moslem militants fighting to overthrow the government and turn Egypt into a strict Islamic state.
Police believe the attack was the work of the Gama'a al-Islamiya (Islamic Group), the largest of the militant organisations, but they have not suggested a motive.
The Interior Ministry, in a statement read on television, said the leader of the group was Farid Salem Abdelkader Kidwani. It did not say how old he was or where he came from.

It said the other suspects were Sayyed Mustafa Ahmed, Hassan Ahmed Abdu, Mohamed Fahmi Abdelrahim Mohamed Ali and Samir Farouk Abdelmuttalib. All four were born between 1968 and 1971 in Abu Qurqas district, within km (miles) of the church.
Moslem and Christian community leaders have unanimously condemned the massacre and security officials have said they believe it was an isolated incident.
It was the worst attack on Christians in Egypt in almost a year and the first time Moslem militants have struck inside a church. The victims were young Copts attending a weekly religious gathering.
The independent Egyptian Human Rights Organisation (EOHR) expressed on Saturday its "extreme condemnation and rejection of this horrific crime".

"By all indications it is a base and premeditated crime aimed primarily at shaking security and the ties and harmony between Moslems and Copts, thereby threatening the state's stability," it added in a statement.

EOHR sent a team of researchers to Abu Qurqas shortly after the attack on a youth meeting in a church there on Wednesday evening. The researchers interviewed survivors of the attack and witnesses but none were able to identify the gunmen.
The group urged the authorities to move the people wounded in the attack to hospitals in Cairo where they could receive better care than in the local state hospital.

Police in southern Egypt suspect the same gunmen who attacked the church also killed three Coptic Christians who were found dead on Friday near Abu Qurqas, in Minya province about 240 km (150 miles) south of Cairo, security sources said.
The Moslem Brotherhood, Egypt's largest political Islamic organistation, said it condemned the "criminal, brute attack".
"We also condemn this irresponsible behaviour, which will lead to insecurity," the Brotherhood said in a statement.

The outlawed and influential group has denied government charges that it is a front for violent groups such as the Gama'a, saying it wants to turn Egypt into an Islamic state through non-violent means such as elections.
Gunmen killed eight Christians in a raid on a farm near the southern city of Assiut in February last year but the motive for that attack was never clear.
The Gama'a has attacked Christians in southern Egypt only sporadically, concentrating attacks on policemen and suspected police informers regardless of religion.

EOHR says 82 Copts have been killed in violent attacks in Egypt since 1992, when the Gama'a began its campaign of violence. Copts make up about 10 percent of Egypt's population. The total number of victims is more than 1,000.
